scope: AQA 7408 Year 1 AS Mechanics 3.4.1.1–3.4.1.6; school Physics mock
notes: Seven independent original worked multi-mark questions, not copied from AQA papers or official mark schemes. Each method/result criterion is a provisional one-mark point and student review may correct automatic marking. Uses a smooth plane; no friction-coefficient calculation.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Horizontal force on a smooth incline with changing normal reaction
questions.prompt: A 4.00 kg block is pushed horizontally towards the top of a fixed smooth plane inclined at 25° to the horizontal. The horizontal push is 35.0 N; use g = 9.81 m s⁻². (a) Resolve the block's weight and the push parallel to the slope. (b) Calculate its acceleration along the plane. (c) Calculate the normal contact force. (d) Find the horizontal push that would instead give zero acceleration along the slope. [8 marks]
markPoints: Weight = mg = 4.00 × 9.81 = 39.24 N vertically down.
The component of weight down the 25° slope is 39.24 sin25° = 16.59 N.
The horizontal 35.0 N push has an up-slope component 35.0 cos25° = 31.72 N.
The resultant parallel force is 31.72 − 16.59 = 15.13 N up the slope.
Newton's second law gives a = 15.13/4.00 = 3.78 m s⁻² up the slope.
The inward normal component of weight is 39.24 cos25° = 35.56 N.
The push adds 35.0 sin25° = 14.79 N into the slope, so the reaction is 50.36 N.
For zero acceleration along the smooth slope, F cos25° = mg sin25°; thus F = mg tan25° = 18.3 N.
questions.modelAnswer: Weight = mg = 4.00 × 9.81 = 39.24 N vertically down. The component of weight down the 25° slope is 39.24 sin25° = 16.59 N. The horizontal 35.0 N push has an up-slope component 35.0 cos25° = 31.72 N. The resultant parallel force is 31.72 − 16.59 = 15.13 N up the slope. Newton's second law gives a = 15.13/4.00 = 3.78 m s⁻² up the slope. The inward normal component of weight is 39.24 cos25° = 35.56 N. The push adds 35.0 sin25° = 14.79 N into the slope, so the reaction is 50.36 N. For zero acceleration along the smooth slope, F cos25° = mg sin25°; thus F = mg tan25° = 18.3 N.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Angled projectile launched from a raised platform
questions.prompt: A ball is launched at 18.0 m s⁻¹ at 40.0° above the horizontal from a platform 12.0 m above level ground. Neglect air resistance; take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate (a) horizontal and vertical components of initial velocity, (b) time before it reaches the ground, (c) horizontal distance from the launch point, and (d) the magnitude and direction of its impact velocity. Show signed vertical working. [8 marks]
markPoints: The initial horizontal velocity is ux = 18.0 cos40° = 13.79 m s⁻¹.
The initial upward velocity is uy = 18.0 sin40° = 11.57 m s⁻¹.
Taking upward as positive and ground height as zero: 0 = 12.0 + 11.57t − 4.905t².
The positive solution of the vertical equation is t = 3.138 s.
Horizontal displacement is x = ux t = 13.79 × 3.138 = 43.3 m.
Vertical impact velocity is vy = uy − gt = −19.22 m s⁻¹.
Impact speed is √(ux² + vy²) = 23.7 m s⁻¹.
Impact direction is tan⁻¹(19.22/13.79) = 54.3° below the horizontal.
questions.modelAnswer: The initial horizontal velocity is ux = 18.0 cos40° = 13.79 m s⁻¹. The initial upward velocity is uy = 18.0 sin40° = 11.57 m s⁻¹. Taking upward as positive and ground height as zero: 0 = 12.0 + 11.57t − 4.905t². The positive solution of the vertical equation is t = 3.138 s. Horizontal displacement is x = ux t = 13.79 × 3.138 = 43.3 m. Vertical impact velocity is vy = uy − gt = −19.22 m s⁻¹. Impact speed is √(ux² + vy²) = 23.7 m s⁻¹. Impact direction is tan⁻¹(19.22/13.79) = 54.3° below the horizontal.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Beam equilibrium with a separately applied couple
questions.prompt: A uniform horizontal beam is 3.00 m long, hinged at its left end, and has weight 60.0 N acting at its centre. An additional 90.0 N downward load acts 2.40 m from the hinge. A taut cable at the right end pulls at 40.0° above the beam towards the left. An external 20.0 N m anticlockwise couple is also applied. The beam is in equilibrium. (a) Find the cable tension using moments about the hinge. (b) Find the vertical and horizontal components of the hinge force and its magnitude. [8 marks]
markPoints: Taking moments about the left hinge eliminates the unknown hinge reaction.
The beam's weight gives 60 × 1.50 = 90 N m clockwise.
The extra downward load gives 90 × 2.40 = 216 N m clockwise; total clockwise moment = 306 N m.
The applied couple contributes 20 N m anticlockwise, whatever the chosen pivot.
Moment equilibrium gives (T sin40°) × 3.00 + 20 = 306, hence T = 148 N.
The cable's upward component is T sin40° = 95.3 N.
Vertical hinge reaction is 60 + 90 − 95.3 = 54.7 N upward.
Horizontal hinge reaction is T cos40° = 113.6 N to the right, giving a resultant reaction of approximately 126 N.
questions.modelAnswer: Taking moments about the left hinge eliminates the unknown hinge reaction. The beam's weight gives 60 × 1.50 = 90 N m clockwise. The extra downward load gives 90 × 2.40 = 216 N m clockwise; total clockwise moment = 306 N m. The applied couple contributes 20 N m anticlockwise, whatever the chosen pivot. Moment equilibrium gives (T sin40°) × 3.00 + 20 = 306, hence T = 148 N. The cable's upward component is T sin40° = 95.3 N. Vertical hinge reaction is 60 + 90 − 95.3 = 54.7 N upward. Horizontal hinge reaction is T cos40° = 113.6 N to the right, giving a resultant reaction of approximately 126 N.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Signed force-time impulses and reversal
questions.prompt: A 0.800 kg trolley initially moves at −0.750 m s⁻¹ along a straight track. Its resultant force–time graph has a positive triangle from t = 0 to 0.100 s, peaking at +100 N, followed by a constant force of −20.0 N from t = 0.100 s to 0.300 s. (a) Find the signed impulse of each section and the total impulse. (b) Determine the final velocity and whether the motion reverses direction. (c) Find the mean resultant force over the 0.300 s. [7 marks]
markPoints: The positive triangular force–time pulse gives impulse ½ × 0.100 × 100 = +5.00 N s.
The later rectangular negative pulse gives impulse (−20.0) × 0.200 = −4.00 N s.
Net impulse over 0.300 s is +1.00 N s, equal to the momentum change.
Initial momentum is 0.800 × (−0.750) = −0.600 kg m s⁻¹.
Final momentum is −0.600 + 1.00 = +0.400 kg m s⁻¹.
Final velocity is +0.400/0.800 = +0.500 m s⁻¹, so the trolley's direction has reversed.
Average resultant force over the full 0.300 s is 1.00/0.300 = +3.33 N.
questions.modelAnswer: The positive triangular force–time pulse gives impulse ½ × 0.100 × 100 = +5.00 N s. The later rectangular negative pulse gives impulse (−20.0) × 0.200 = −4.00 N s. Net impulse over 0.300 s is +1.00 N s, equal to the momentum change. Initial momentum is 0.800 × (−0.750) = −0.600 kg m s⁻¹. Final momentum is −0.600 + 1.00 = +0.400 kg m s⁻¹. Final velocity is +0.400/0.800 = +0.500 m s⁻¹, so the trolley's direction has reversed. Average resultant force over the full 0.300 s is 1.00/0.300 = +3.33 N.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Velocity-time reversal, displacement and distance
questions.prompt: A particle's velocity–time graph has straight lines from (0 s, −6 m s⁻¹) to (3 s, +6 m s⁻¹), then stays at +6 m s⁻¹ until t = 5 s, then falls linearly to −2 m s⁻¹ at t = 9 s. (a) Find its acceleration from 0 to 3 s. (b) Find both times at which the particle changes direction. (c) Calculate net displacement and total distance travelled over 0–9 s, explaining how negative areas are treated. [8 marks]
markPoints: Acceleration over 0–3 s is (6 − (−6))/3 = +4.0 m s⁻².
Velocity crosses zero at t = 1.5 s and again at t = 8.0 s.
The signed displacement from 0–3 s is zero because equal positive and negative triangular areas cancel.
From 3–5 s displacement is +6 × 2 = +12 m.
From 5–9 s signed displacement is ½(6 + (−2)) × 4 = +8 m.
Net displacement over 0–9 s is 0 + 12 + 8 = +20 m.
Distance in 0–3 s is two positive triangle magnitudes: 2 × (½ × 1.5 × 6) = 9 m.
Distance in 5–9 s is ½ × 3 × 6 + ½ × 1 × 2 = 10 m; total distance is 9 + 12 + 10 = 31 m.
questions.modelAnswer: Acceleration over 0–3 s is (6 − (−6))/3 = +4.0 m s⁻². Velocity crosses zero at t = 1.5 s and again at t = 8.0 s. The signed displacement from 0–3 s is zero because equal positive and negative triangular areas cancel. From 3–5 s displacement is +6 × 2 = +12 m. From 5–9 s signed displacement is ½(6 + (−2)) × 4 = +8 m. Net displacement over 0–9 s is 0 + 12 + 8 = +20 m. Distance in 0–3 s is two positive triangle magnitudes: 2 × (½ × 1.5 × 6) = 9 m. Distance in 5–9 s is ½ × 3 × 6 + ½ × 1 × 2 = 10 m; total distance is 9 + 12 + 10 = 31 m.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Perfectly inelastic collision and mean interaction force
questions.prompt: Two trolleys on a level low-friction track collide and stick together. Trolley A has mass 0.300 kg and velocity +4.00 m s⁻¹; trolley B has mass 0.500 kg and velocity −2.00 m s⁻¹. The interaction lasts 0.100 s. (a) Find their common velocity. (b) Find the total kinetic energy before and after and state whether kinetic energy is conserved. (c) Determine the average force on each trolley during the collision, with signs. [8 marks]
markPoints: Before collision the total signed momentum is (0.300 × 4.00) + (0.500 × (−2.00)) = +0.200 kg m s⁻¹.
Conservation of momentum gives combined final velocity 0.200/(0.300 + 0.500) = +0.250 m s⁻¹.
Initial total kinetic energy is ½(0.300)(4.00²) + ½(0.500)(2.00²) = 3.40 J.
Final kinetic energy is ½(0.800)(0.250²) = 0.0250 J.
Kinetic energy lost from the trolleys is 3.40 − 0.0250 = 3.375 J; kinetic energy is not conserved in this inelastic collision.
Trolley A's momentum change is 0.300(0.250 − 4.00) = −1.125 N s.
Over 0.100 s the average force on A from B is −1.125/0.100 = −11.25 N.
By Newton's third law, the simultaneous average force on B from A is +11.25 N (equal and opposite).
questions.modelAnswer: Before collision the total signed momentum is (0.300 × 4.00) + (0.500 × (−2.00)) = +0.200 kg m s⁻¹. Conservation of momentum gives combined final velocity 0.200/(0.300 + 0.500) = +0.250 m s⁻¹. Initial total kinetic energy is ½(0.300)(4.00²) + ½(0.500)(2.00²) = 3.40 J. Final kinetic energy is ½(0.800)(0.250²) = 0.0250 J. Kinetic energy lost from the trolleys is 3.40 − 0.0250 = 3.375 J; kinetic energy is not conserved in this inelastic collision. Trolley A's momentum change is 0.300(0.250 − 4.00) = −1.125 N s. Over 0.100 s the average force on A from B is −1.125/0.100 = −11.25 N. By Newton's third law, the simultaneous average force on B from A is +11.25 N (equal and opposite).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Variable drag, terminal speed and deceleration
questions.prompt: A 70.0 kg object falls vertically through air. Take g = 9.80 m s⁻², and choose downward as positive. At one instant upward drag is 440 N. (a) Find the resultant force and acceleration. (b) State the drag needed for constant terminal speed. (c) At another instant the upward drag is 750 N while the object still moves downward. Find its acceleration and explain what happens to its speed. [7 marks]
markPoints: The object's weight is mg = 70.0 × 9.80 = 686 N downward.
When drag is 440 N upwards, the resultant is 686 − 440 = 246 N downward.
Newton's second law gives downward acceleration 246/70.0 = 3.51 m s⁻².
At terminal speed, zero resultant force requires an upward drag force of 686 N.
If drag becomes 750 N upward, the signed downward resultant is 686 − 750 = −64 N.
The signed downward acceleration then is −64/70.0 = −0.914 m s⁻² (equivalently 0.914 m s⁻² upward).
The object can still be moving down while accelerating up, in which case its downward speed decreases; drag generally increases with speed.
questions.modelAnswer: The object's weight is mg = 70.0 × 9.80 = 686 N downward. When drag is 440 N upwards, the resultant is 686 − 440 = 246 N downward. Newton's second law gives downward acceleration 246/70.0 = 3.51 m s⁻². At terminal speed, zero resultant force requires an upward drag force of 686 N. If drag becomes 750 N upward, the signed downward resultant is 686 − 750 = −64 N. The signed downward acceleration then is −64/70.0 = −0.914 m s⁻² (equivalently 0.914 m s⁻² upward). The object can still be moving down while accelerating up, in which case its downward speed decreases; drag generally increases with speed.
